one_liner: Rust SIMD image-resampling crate with 30+ filters and colour-space-aware scaling; no valid speed comparison against fast_image_resize exists.
what_it_does: pic-scale resizes in-memory images: u8, u16 (up to 16-bit), i16, f32 and nightly f16 pixels as RGBA, RGB, gray+alpha, CbCr and single planes, plus AR30/RA30. You build a Scaler with a ResamplingFunction (Lanczos3/4/5, Mitchell, CatmullRom, EWA and Jinc variants, Box, Nearest and others), call plan_*_resampling(source, target, premultiply) once, then run plan.resample or resample_with_scratch repeatedly on caller-allocated ImageStore buffers. The optional 'colorspaces' feature adds scalers that resize in linear light, Lab, Luv, LCh, Oklab, Jzazbz, XYZ or sigmoidal space. The picscale/ subcrate builds a static library with a cbindgen C++ header (enum class, constexpr), but it exposes only six filters, takes a flags word and builds only with nightly Rust.
how_it_is_fast: It does separable convolution with per-output weight tables computed once at plan time and quantised to fixed point. On x86 the u8 paths use Q15 i16 weights with _mm256_madd_epi16 into i32 (SSE4.1 and AVX2 runtime-dispatched; AVX-VNNI under the avx512 feature). On aarch64 the default WorkloadStrategy::PreferSpeed switches to cheaper arithmetic: with RDM (scale below 8) pixels are shifted left 6 bits into i16 and multiplied with vqrdmulh, and with the nightly_i8mm feature on an i8mm CPU (scale below 10) both passes use Q0.7 int8 weights and vusdot dot products. Rows are processed four at a time, and an optional novtb thread pool splits rows when ThreadingPolicy is Fixed or Adaptive. Optional supersampling pre-shrinks large downscales (3x or more) with Box or Nearest before the quality filter.
when_to_use: Rust code that needs gamma-correct or perceptual resizing (linear light, Oklab, Lab, sigmoidal) without writing the conversion passes yourself.
Pipelines with formats most resizers lack: f16 (nightly), AR30/RA30 10-bit packed, 10/12/16-bit u16 with an explicit bit depth, signed i16 planes, or YUV chroma (CbCr) planes.
Repeated resizes of the same geometry (video frames, tiles), where one plan plus a reused scratch buffer avoids recomputing weights and allocating per call.
Apple Silicon or other ARMv8.2+/v8.6 hosts where a lower-precision fast path is acceptable for thumbnails (RDM by default, i8mm with nightly_i8mm).
Projects that already pull it in transitively: its largest crates.io dependent is the hayro PDF renderer (hayro 0.7.1 alone has about 1.26 million downloads).
when_not_to_use: When you need a measured speed advantage: no valid published comparison exists. The old README table was taken on a Lanczos3 kernel at half the correct support (fixed in v0.6.12), and the current speedtest commits no results.

When output must be bit-exact across CPUs or match a reference: the default PreferSpeed mode picks different arithmetic per ISA (Q0.7 int8 weights on i8mm ARM, RDM i16 on ARMv8.1+, Q15 i16 on x86), and issue #161 (Aug 2026) found SIMD and scalar results diverging; set WorkloadStrategy::PreferQuality if this matters.

Releases before 0.7.12: issue #161 listed a sign-bit loss in the SSE f32-to-f16 fallback that corrupted Lanczos output with negative taps, an out-of-bounds read in a NEON f16 row kernel, Miri-flagged misaligned NEON loads and an SVE2 kernel that assumed 128-bit vectors. These were fixed in PR #164 (merged 2026-09-10, the day 0.7.12 was published). Issue #150 (an all-zero last row on a 1x5 to 2x5 CatmullRom resize) was fixed in PR #151 in May 2026.
C or C++ code bases that want a stable, documented library: the C++ header needs a nightly Rust build with -Z build-std, and covers six filters only. zimg (C++) or libvips are more natural there.
Stable-Rust users who need f16, i8mm or SVE paths: those sit behind nightly-only features.

integration.form: crate (plus an optional static library with a C++ header from the picscale/ subcrate)
integration.dependencies: num-traits, pxfm; optional novtb (threading, on by default) and colorutils-rs (colorspaces feature)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.89 (rust-version in Cargo.toml, edition 2024); nightly for nightly_f16, nightly_i8mm, nightly_avx512fp16, sve and for building the C bindings
integration.platforms: x86-64 and i686 (SSE4.1 and AVX2 detected at run time; AVX-512/AVX-VNNI with the avx512 feature), aarch64 NEON (RDM, i8mm, fp16 detected at run time; SVE2 partial), wasm32 with simd128 enabled at compile time, scalar fallback elsewhere (CI builds powerpc and riscv64)
integration.thread_safety: Plans are returned as Arc<dyn ResamplingPlan + Send + Sync> and resample through &self, so one plan can serve several threads, each with its own scratch and destination (from reading the source; not stated in the README). Internal threading is off by default (ThreadingPolicy::Single); Fixed(n) or Adaptive opt in.

gotchas: SIMD is a cargo feature, not automatic: default-features = false (for example to drop the novtb threading dependency) turns off neon, rdm, sse and avx and leaves scalar code only. zenresize's paired_bench documents this ('by default pic-scale builds scalar-only') because it depends on pic-scale with default features off.

WorkloadStrategy::PreferSpeed is the default. On ARM it trades precision for speed (RDM i16 path, or Q0.7 int8 weights when nightly_i8mm is on), and the source comments warn that the RDM path 'won't work really well on huge kernel'. On x86, PreferSpeed turns the AVX-VNNI horizontal u8 kernel off.

With ThreadingPolicy::Fixed or Adaptive, a new novtb pool is constructed for each filter pass of every call rather than reused. Adaptive uses one thread per 65,536 output pixels, capped at available_parallelism.
The README example still uses LinearScaler, which needs the non-default 'colorspaces' feature. It also mentions a 'nightly_avx512' feature that Cargo.toml names 'avx512'.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over fast_image_resize when you need colour-space-aware scaling, f16/AR30/CbCr formats, built-in threading or the exotic EWA/Jinc filters. fast_image_resize is the safer choice for plain 8-bit resizing, because it has reproducible numbers against libvips, the image crate and the resize crate, while pic-scale has none. In C++ projects, zimg or stb-image-resize-opt avoid a nightly Rust build.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing valid is measured. Up to v0.6.11 the README showed a Lanczos3 4x-downscale table against fast_image_resize (for example RGB 10.47 vs 15.62 with AVX2; units and rustc version not given). Those runs used a kernel at half the correct Lanczos3 support, so pic-scale did about half the work, and commit 30b40e5 (v0.6.12) fixed the kernel and deleted the table. The current speedtest harness (4928x3279 RGBA8, single thread on both sides, geometric mean after 10 warm-ups) publishes no results.
status_note: Actively maintained by one author (last commit and 0.7.12 release 2026-09-10, 803 commits, 0 open issues) and dual BSD-3-Clause/Apache-2.0, so copyable; it has only 41 stars, and its crates.io volume comes largely from dependents such as hayro. Treat any speed claim as unmeasured until someone publishes a like-for-like run.
measurement_notes: Builds on the verifier's findings (half-support Lanczos3 behind the old README table; width x width fast_image_resize destination in speedtest/src/runner.rs). New for the orchestrator: (1) The speedtest crate enables pic-scale features rdm and nightly_i8mm and keeps the default WorkloadStrategy::PreferSpeed. src/factory/rgba_u8.rs and src/factory/rgb_u8.rs (vertical_strategy_u8) then pick, on aarch64, Q0.7 int8 weights with vusdot dot products for both passes whenever the CPU reports i8mm and the scale factor is below 10, or the RDM path (pixels << 6 in i16, vqrdmulh, documented in src/neon/rgba_u8_rdm.rs as 'slightly lower precision') for scale below 8. fast_image_resize uses i16 weights with i32 accumulation. Any ARM chart from that harness therefore compares a lower-precision kernel against a higher-precision one, on top of the destination-size bug. On x86 AVX2 both libraries use Q15/i16 weights with madd into i32, so precision there is comparable. (2) Issue #161 (2026-08-23) documented real correctness bugs in released SIMD paths: the SSE f32-to-f16 fallback dropped the sign bit (corrupting Lanczos output with negative taps), a NEON f16 row kernel read out of bounds (jx <= size), Miri found misaligned NEON loads and out-of-bounds reads in vertical_f32 for narrow widths, and the SVE2 dot kernel hard-coded 128-bit offsets. All were fixed in PR #164 (merged 2026-09-10; 0.7.12 was published the same day). Some (the SSE/AVX2 divide-by-255 rounding and the misaligned NEON loads) touched u8 kernels; they bear on output correctness; the only published numbers (the u8 RGB/RGBA table up to v0.6.11) are already invalid because of the half-support kernel. (3) imazen/zenresize's paired_bench depends on pic-scale with default-features = false, which makes pic-scale scalar-only unless its bench-simd-competitors feature is on, as its README warns. Any zenresize result taken without that flag would understate pic-scale. No zenresize result file compares the two yet. None of this changes tier D.
